source.title: Katherine Ryan says she feels 'grief and relief' after Russell Brand conviction
source.summary: The comedian had previously spoken about an unnamed "predator" in the entertainment industry.
source.evidence_text:
Comedian Katherine Ryan has said she feels "grief and relief" after Russell Brand was convicted of rape and sexual assault.
Brand was found guilty on Thursday of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.
Speaking about the guilty verdict of his trial, on the latest episode of her podcast Telling Everybody Everything, Ryan said: "It really made me feel just quite dysregulated again, caught off-guard, emotional, in awe of the survivors who also had nothing to gain.
"I just think again and again about people who have been hurt, and who have to carry that, who've carried that around long enough, and will continue to carry that in some way, regardless of what justice is done."
The 51-year-old will be sentenced on Monday. The judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, told him to expect "a significant custodial term" after the verdicts were delivered.
The former entertainer was acquitted of two other rape charges and one allegation of attempted indecent assault.
"They came forward despite Russell Brand having fame, power, money, and a legion of fans ready to attack them."
Ryan had previously claimed in a BBC TV documentary interview with Louis Theroux that there was a "predator" in the entertainment industry.
Ryan said in 2022 that she could not name the famous man as it would be a "litigious minefield" but mentioned that she had appeared on a TV programme with him and told him he was a "predator" to "his face".
It was widely rumoured Ryan had been referring to her time on Comedy Central's Roast Battle in 2018 alongside Brand, but she has not confirmed she was referring to him, and she did not name the show she was working on.
Brand is now also being investigated over further rape allegations made by two women, police have now said.
The Canadian stand-up and TV star said there were "a lot of women speaking privately and quietly" following Thursday's verdict, who feel "a very nuanced mix of emotions".
She added: "I will never be someone who like, dances on graves. There has been some justice done today. There's a level of relief, but there's grief alongside relief.
During a pre-trial hearing in October Brand tried unsuccessfully to have his criminal case thrown out.
His lawyers argued that the actor and entertainer couldn't receive a fair trial because of the publicity following the Dispatches programme.
Ryan's comments came on the same day that former BBC One controller Lorraine Heggessey questioned how and why Brand was able to "get away with it so long?
"He brought in a young audience, which a lot of broadcasters crave. So I think all of those reasons... and as people have said, he did hide in plain sight."

discussion: Why can Ryan feel relief and still feel sad? Use “She can feel both because ...”.
Imagine a friend feels sad after hearing news like this. What could you say to help? Use “I could say ... because ...”.

vocabulary.definition: Involving subtle differences or layers, as when several emotions coexist and a single label would oversimplify them.
A situation in which what someone says or does could expose them to legal action, with risks that are difficult to anticipate or manage.
Discussion about what might be true when the available information leaves the answer uncertain.
Feeling deep admiration or respect for someone, here for the courage the survivors showed.
The possibility of a future event that someone has reason to take seriously.
An individual charge in a criminal case that can receive its own verdict.
A formal legal expression for a period of imprisonment imposed as part of a sentence.
Formally ended by a court, here in reference to the outcome Brand unsuccessfully sought before trial.
Likely to undermine the fairness of a legal proceeding, for example by influencing people’s views before they hear the evidence.
Made to answer for one’s conduct and face any consequences that follow.
Strongly want something considered valuable, here an audience of younger viewers.

grammar.explanation: Use “however much” before an uncountable noun to introduce a clause meaning “no matter how much”. The amount can vary without changing the outcome in the main clause. Here, the effects of harm persist whatever degree of justice is achieved.
grammar.example_quote: However much justice is done, Ryan said, those who were hurt will continue to live with the consequences.

quiz.question: Which contrast in Ryan’s comments helps explain how grief and relief can coexist?
options: The court reached a decision, while the women who spoke privately were still waiting for a ruling.
The conviction represents a measure of justice, while those who were hurt continue to live with the consequences.

option_feedback: The brief describes the private conversations as reactions to the verdict. Ryan’s contrast concerns what a court can deliver and what people continue to live with.
Ryan acknowledges that some justice was done and says that those who were hurt will continue to live with the consequences.
The brief reports both outcomes at trial. Ryan’s comments contrast the justice achieved with the harm that persists.

quiz.question: What concern did Ryan express by describing the act of naming the man as a “litigious minefield”?

The main risk in naming him was that it would reveal the programme they had appeared on.

option_feedback: “Litigious minefield” signals legal risks that are difficult to navigate. Whether anyone would take legal action remains open.
The programme’s identity was also uncertain, but “litigious” points to the risk of legal action.
“Litigious” signals the possibility of legal action, and “minefield” suggests that the risks are difficult to navigate.

quiz.question: What does the brief establish about the suggested link between Ryan’s earlier remarks and Roast Battle?

Ryan identified Roast Battle as the programme and left the man’s identity open.

quiz.question: What does “the prospect of attacks” imply about the situation Ryan described?

Ryan saw the risk of attacks as arising only after the court ruled.

Ryan links the risk to the survivors coming forward. The sentence gives no timetable for when attacks might occur.
“Prospect” presents attacks as a possibility that the survivors faced when they came forward.

quiz.question: In “one count of rape”, what does “count” refer to?

A single criminal charge on which the court could return a verdict.
A separate prison term imposed for a particular offence.

Each “count” is an individual charge that the court can decide separately.
A “count” is a charge the court decides. A prison term is a possible consequence of a conviction.

quiz.question: What did the judge tell Brand to expect at sentencing?
options: A substantial prison term, with the precise length still unspecified in the brief.
A formal announcement of the length of a prison term that had already been imposed.
A possible prison term, with no indication of how substantial it might be.
option_feedback: The judge indicated both the type and likely scale of the sentence. The brief gives no specific duration.
The judge was telling Brand what to expect ahead of Monday’s sentencing, when the sentence was due to be imposed.
The judge told Brand to expect a substantial term, which gives an indication of its likely scale.

quiz.question: What claim did Brand’s lawyers make about the publicity following the Dispatches programme?
options: They argued that the publicity made the further allegations a matter for the same trial.
They argued that the publicity would make a fair trial more difficult but still possible.
They argued that the publicity made a fair trial impossible.

The lawyers’ claim was stronger. They argued that the publicity was so prejudicial that Brand could not receive a fair trial.

The scheduled sentencing concerns the conviction. The brief gives no indication of when the investigation will conclude.

options: She suggests that his appeal to a sought-after audience may help explain why he avoided accountability for so long.
She treats the age of his viewers as evidence about the offences considered at trial.
